texts.label: text
texts.orig: An ideal gas is a model in which the molecules are point particles that never interact except in brief elastic collisions. Its pressure, volume and temperature obey the ideal gas law, PV = NkT, where N is the number of molecules and k is the Boltzmann constant. The model works well for dilute gases far from condensation, such as helium or argon at room temperature and ordinary pressure, and it is the reference system against which real gases are compared in the rest of these notes here.

Its pressure, volume and temperature obey the ideal gas law, PV = NkT, where N is the number of molecules and k is the Boltzmann constant. texts.label: text
texts.orig: Boyle observed that at constant temperature the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is inversely proportional to its volume: halving the volume of the container doubles the pressure. Charles found that at constant pressure the volume grows linearly with temperature. Both empirical laws are special cases of the ideal gas law and were historically the evidence that led to it, long before the molecular picture of a gas was accepted by chemists.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Real gases deviate from this simple behaviour at high density, where molecules are close together.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas law for two effects that the ideal model ignores. First, molecules occupy a finite excluded volume, so the volume available to each molecule is reduced by a constant b per mole. Second, molecules attract one another at moderate distances, which lowers the pressure exerted on the walls by an amount proportional to a over the square of the molar volume. The resulting equation of state predicts a critical point, below whose temperature the isotherms develop a loop that signals the coexistence of liquid and vapour. Maxwell's equal area construction replaces the loop by a flat segment at the vapour pressure. The van der Waals constants a and b are fitted to measured critical data for each substance, and the theory then gives a qualitative account of condensation, although the predicted critical compressibility ratio is not accurate for most real fluids.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Kinetic theory explains the ideal gas law from the motion of molecules. In equilibrium the molecular speeds follow the Maxwell distribution, whose shape depends only on the temperature and the molecular mass. The mean kinetic energy per molecule is three halves of kT, independent of the mass, so heavier molecules move more slowly on average. The root mean square speed of nitrogen at room temperature is about five hundred metres per second. Collisions with the walls transfer momentum, and averaging that transfer over the Maxwell distribution recovers the pressure of the ideal gas law. Between collisions a molecule travels a mean free path that grows as the density falls, which sets the scale for viscosity, diffusion and thermal conduction in dilute gases. Effusion through a small hole, studied by Graham, selects faster molecules and was used to separate isotopes. All of these results follow from treating the molecules as independent classical particles with random velocities, the same assumptions that define the ideal gas.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Pressure is the momentum delivered per unit time and per unit area by molecules striking the walls of the container. Each impact reverses the normal component of a molecular velocity, and the rate of impacts grows with density and speed, so pressure grows with both.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure by the height of a mercury column, about seven hundred sixty millimetres at sea level. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal, one newton per square metre, and one standard atmosphere is about one hundred kilopascals.
